forces: Two solo violins and solo cello, ripieno strings and basso continuo
performers: Advent Chamber Orchestra; Roxanna Pavel Goldstein, musical director
question: When a span repeats, can you shift attention from the violin line to the bass?
intro: Four slow bars open this concerto’s first movement before the fast violin lines enter in imitation. The Allegro repeats each of its two main spans, letting the ear hear the same exchanges twice.

cues.title: Four slow bars before the Allegro
cues.text: The introduction uses chordal phrases and rests to establish the key. Its last held harmony delays the fast movement: the Allegro’s flowing violin line is a change in both tempo and texture.
cues.evidence: The inspected full score begins Concerto IV with four Adagio bars followed by Allegro at bar 5. The report’s 0:20 boundary separates low onset activity from rapid attacks: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5e/IMSLP128514-PMLP28008-Corelli_-_Op._6.pdf, PDF page 65, printed page 56.

cues.title: One violin line answers another
cues.text: The fast section begins with imitative violin writing. Listen for the second line taking up the first line’s kind of motion, rather than for a solo melody accompanied only by chords. The texture can grow from the interaction of related lines.
cues.evidence: The score’s Allegro begins with the concertino violins entering in succession. The report’s onset rate rises from about 0.6–0.8 per second in the introduction to 4.4–6 around 0:20–0:30: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5e/IMSLP128514-PMLP28008-Corelli_-_Op._6.pdf, printed page 56.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first strain again
cues.text: The first fast span repeats, without bringing back the slow introduction. Try following the bass this time while the violin figures remain familiar; repetition gives a second view of the same musical construction.
cues.evidence: The score repeats the first Allegro strain through bar 25. The report’s level, brightness and pitch-content contours at approximately 1:00–1:35 closely resemble 0:20–0:55, with a change around 0:58: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5e/IMSLP128514-PMLP28008-Corelli_-_Op._6.pdf, printed pages 56–58.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A publication after Corelli’s death
cues.text: Corelli’s twelve concerti grossi, Op. 6, appeared in Amsterdam in 1714, after his death in 1713. This recording presents only the opening movement of the fourth concerto, not the whole four-movement work.
cues.evidence: The collection catalogue gives the 1714 Amsterdam publication and identifies Corelli’s dates; the individual work catalogue lists four movements: https://imslp.org/wiki/12_Concerti_Grossi,_Op.6_(Corelli,_Arcangelo); https://imslp.org/wiki/Concerto_grosso_in_D_major,_Op.6_No.4_(Corelli,_Arcangelo).

cues.title: Small group and larger group
cues.text: The original title distinguishes two violins and cello in the concertino from the larger ripieno string body. The larger group could be reinforced: the contrast lies in musical function, not in a permanently fixed modern orchestra size.
cues.evidence: The 1714 collection title specifies the two obbligato violins and cello and the ripieno parts, which can be doubled: https://imslp.org/wiki/12_Concerti_Grossi,_Op.6_(Corelli,_Arcangelo). No exact player count is claimed for this recording.

cues.title: Hear the second route twice
cues.text: The second strain repeats its contrasting exchanges before closing again in D major. Listen for the repeated route through the phrase rather than assuming that every renewed violin figure is a new section.
cues.evidence: The score’s second Allegro strain, bars 26–51, is repeated. The report shows similar pitch-content and texture profiles beginning around 1:42 and 2:32, then D-major-compatible closing regions around 2:10–2:20 and 3:05–3:15: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5e/IMSLP128514-PMLP28008-Corelli_-_Op._6.pdf, printed pages 59–61.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The source identifies a season
cues.text: The Advent Chamber Orchestra source places this performance among selections from its 2005–2006 season and credits Roxanna Pavel Goldstein as musical director. It does not supply an exact concert date or name the concertino players.
cues.evidence: The Commons description reproduces the season and leadership credits from the Al Goldstein/Pandora Music source. Musical director is retained as the documented role, not silently changed to conductor: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Corelli_-_Concerto_Grosso_Op._6_No._4_-_1._Adagio_-_Allegro.ogg.

transitions.title: A held dominant releases the running line
transitions.how: The slow introduction reaches a held A-major harmony, the dominant of D. The first concertino violin then begins the Allegro’s flowing figure, followed by another violin line. The tempo change and staggered entries replace the opening’s chordal weight with imitation.
transitions.evidence: The score’s fourth bar holds the dominant before Allegro at bar 5. The report’s strongest boundary is 0:20 and its onset density rises sharply there: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5e/IMSLP128514-PMLP28008-Corelli_-_Op._6.pdf, printed page 56.

transitions.title: The cadence sends the fast span back
transitions.how: The first strain closes in A major and returns directly to the beginning of the Allegro. The four-bar Adagio is left behind. Recognising the returning violin figure makes the repeat audible even though the music does not pause to announce it.
transitions.evidence: The score closes the first strain at bar 25 with a repeat. The report’s 0:58–1:02 changes begin a contour resembling the first traversal from 0:20: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5e/IMSLP128514-PMLP28008-Corelli_-_Op._6.pdf, printed pages 56–58.

transitions.title: The second ending moves into new exchanges
transitions.how: After the first strain’s dominant-key close has been heard again, the next span continues with new exchanges between the violin lines. The fast pulse persists while the harmony moves onwards, eventually returning to D major for the movement’s close.
transitions.evidence: The second strain begins at score bar 26 and closes at bar 51. The report has a strong boundary at 1:42 and changed pitch content in the following windows; this is not a key claim derived from the estimator alone: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5e/IMSLP128514-PMLP28008-Corelli_-_Op._6.pdf, printed pages 59–61.

transitions.title: A tonic close begins the second repeat
transitions.how: The second strain reaches D major, then repeats its own opening rather than returning to the start of the movement. Its imitative exchanges and final cadence are heard again, giving both the outward motion and the homecoming a second traversal.
transitions.evidence: The inspected score repeats the second Allegro strain. The report marks 2:32, with later contours resembling the first traversal from 1:42. The recording’s final decay follows the repeated close: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5e/IMSLP128514-PMLP28008-Corelli_-_Op._6.pdf, printed pages 59–61.

source.title: Corelli, Op. 6 — full score, Concerto IV
source.locator: Printed pages 56–61. The single solo-violin desk groups both concertino violin lines; cellos groups concertino cello and ripieno bass participation. This is a functional passage overview, not an inventory of players or a claim about a recorded keyboard realization.

timeline.note: Concertino and ripieno contribute to the slow chordal introduction.
The first concertino violin starts the Allegro; the second violin line follows. Both are represented by this one desk.
The imitation expands into concertino/ripieno exchanges; the display groups the passage rather than claiming continuous playing by every part.
The first strain restarts with the concertino violin entry pattern.
The repeated passage again broadens into the larger string texture.
Second-strain exchanges and alternating string density; part participation is intermittent.
The second strain repeats and returns to its D-major close.
